summary:
AstroHealth — Space Station Crew Health Monitoring System

Problem: In microgravity and cosmic radiation, astronauts experience rapid muscle atrophy, bone loss, and metabolic shifts. Flight surgeons and crew need immediate, actionable health and environmental insights without information overload—and a system that easily integrates new sensors without costly rewrites.

Solution: AstroHealth is a full-stack platform combining astronaut biometrics with shared station telemetry (radiation, microgravity, air/surface microbes). It enforces strict role-based access:

Astronaut View: Personal health trends, lab panels, interactive 2D body maps (muscle/bone loss), sleep scoring, and a supportive wellbeing journal.

Flight Surgeon View: A station-wide crew dashboard prioritized by alert severity.

Full-width alert banners flag out-of-range metrics or overdue tests across all tabs. Clicking an alert jumps directly to the relevant chart or highlights the affected muscle/bone on the 2D body map.

Technical Innovation: Powered by a Rust hexagonal backend, PostgreSQL 16, and a React 19 / TypeScript / Mantine frontend. Its core advantage is declarative modularity: adding a new metric requires just 1 definition file and 1 line in the catalog—automatically creating a DB partition, validating data, computing alerts, and rendering the UI widget.
details:
AstroHealth – Space Station Crew Health Monitoring System

What it does and how it works

AstroHealth is a visual tool that reduces astronauts' cognitive load. It automatically monitors large volumes of health data in the background (mental health data is deliberately excluded from automatic analysis). It identifies concerning results and tells astronauts when a health test is due or when a specific parameter needs attention. Users don't have to interpret complex medical data themselves: the tool highlights the most relevant information and presents it in an accessible way. Full details of all monitored data remain available whenever needed.

The platform combines astronaut biometrics with shared station telemetry. It tracks physiological parameters (resting heart rate, body temperature, blood pressure, muscle atrophy, bone density loss, blood and urine panels, sleep quality) and station environment data (airborne and surface microbes, radiation dose rate, residual gravity). Every reading is checked against reference ranges based on ISS limits, typical laboratory ranges and WHO T-score criteria, and gets a status: normal, warning or critical. Alerts are calculated automatically.

Out-of-range results and overdue measurements appear as full-width banners at the top of the screen, sorted by severity and visible from every tab. Clicking an alert jumps to the right report, highlights the affected chart and, on an interactive 2D body map, marks the exact muscle or bone involved. Muscle atrophy is shown as a percentage change from each astronaut's pre-flight baseline, so every crew member is compared with themselves, not with an average. Sleep gets a 0–100 score with a report of the last night.

The system has two strictly separated roles:

Astronaut view: personal health trends, lab panels, body maps, sleep score and a supportive wellbeing note. Astronauts see only their own data.

Flight surgeon view: a station-wide crew dashboard sorted from the most urgent case, with access to each crew member's full profile.

Access rules are enforced in the backend, not only in the user interface.

Benefits and intended impact

In microgravity and under cosmic radiation, astronauts experience rapid muscle atrophy, bone loss and metabolic shifts. On long missions, especially to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean crews must catch health problems early and on their own. AstroHealth turns scattered measurements into a clear picture: what is fine, what is getting worse and what needs action now. Trends over 30 days, 90 days or the whole mission help spot slow processes like bone and muscle loss before they become dangerous.

Our innovation is not collecting or displaying health data, but changing how astronauts interact with it. We designed the tool so that astronauts don't have to work as medical-data analysts on top of their already demanding responsibilities.

How the project is creative

We treated each health parameter as data, not as code. Adding a new metric takes one declarative definition file (name, units, normal ranges, chart type, measurement interval) and one line in the catalog. From that, the system automatically creates the database partition, validation, statuses, alerts, the dashboard widget, the crew table column and demo data. Adding a new tab takes one line. New sensors and medical tests can be integrated as missions change, without costly rewrites.

We also designed the interface to calm people rather than alarm them. Alerts appear only where they matter, and a green "all parameters normal" bar shows when nothing needs attention.

Tools and technologies

Backend: Rust (axum, tokio, sqlx) in a hexagonal architecture, JWT authentication and Argon2 password hashing.

Database: PostgreSQL 16 with a separate partition for each parameter's history.

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Mantine UI and Recharts, plus a custom SVG body map.

Deployment: Docker Compose.

Measurements come in through a device-ingestion interface, so real wearables and lab equipment can be connected later.

Demo data simulates realistic scenarios, such as a solar storm raising radiation levels and progressive calf muscle loss.

Our development process combined extensive human deliberation with the use of LLMs to generate the code. Humans defined the problem, evaluated design decisions, identified risks and set the application's underlying logic. LLMs supported the technical implementation.

Factors we considered

Clarity under stress, privacy between crew members, a clear separation between astronaut and flight-surgeon access, modularity for future sensors, and realistic medical reference ranges (approximations, not clinical advice).

We also considered automatically analysing astronauts' mental health, but concluded it could not be done reliably. Mental health is hard to assess from facial expressions, body language, speech or writing, so astronauts' own openness is crucial. Our reasons:

Individual and cultural differences: astronauts from different cultures express and mask emotions differently. Reliable analysis would need individual calibration and personalised neural network training.

Emotional masking: astronauts are trained to stay composed under pressure, so visible emotional cues can be misleading. When distressed, they may also consciously change how they speak or write, which makes them harder to interpret.

Physiological changes: microgravity changes facial appearance, so neural networks trained on Earth may give wrong results.

Constant surveillance: continuous mental health monitoring could itself increase stress.

That is why mental wellbeing appears only as a gentle, supportive note that never triggers alarms.
